sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Rongo** ​(*rongo*) — ‌Agriculture, Peace, ‌Cultivated Foods ​· Peace, ​news (from ​Proto-Polynesian *longo) ​— belongs ​to the ‌Polynesian ​tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued under ​the domain ‌"Agriculture, Peace, ​Cultivated Foods". ‌The name ​means "Peace, ​news ​(from Proto-Polynesian ​*longo)"[^1].

Rongo ​is the ‌**Māori god ​of cultivated ‌foods and ​of peace** ‌— ​the kūmara ‌in the ​ground, the ‌stored harvest, ​the quiet ​field. One ‌of the ‌sons of ‌Ranginui ​and Papatūānuku, ​he is ‌the brother ​who hid ​from the ‌storm inside ​the Earth ​and became, ‌in ​the people's ‌telling, the ​very food ​dug from ​her bosom. ​Across Polynesia ‌his name ‌resounds as ​Hawaiian ‌Lono and ​Tahitian Ro'o: ​the god ‌of what ‌is planted.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ​scholarly spelling ‌**Rongo** ​and serves ​its temple ​at [its ‌temple](https://punicodex.com/rongo/). The ​displayed form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ‌description ​computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*rongo* contains ​the same ‌letters: no ​recovered ‌diacritics or ‌special encoding ​is claimed. ​The work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in modern ​Polynesian ​orthographies; ​macron usage ​follows ​each tradition’s ‌reference ​dictionaries. Etymologically ​the ‌name ​means "Peace, ‌news ​(from Proto-Polynesian ‌*longo)"[^1].

​The reconstructed ​proto-form ​is ​*longo* (proto-polynesian, ​"Peace, ‌news"). Peace, ​news ‌(from Proto-Polynesian ​*longo)

‌The ​canonical spelling ‌**Rongo** ​matches the ‌conventional ​scholarly romanization. ​The ‌plain ‌ASCII form ‌*rongo* ​contains the ​same ‌letters, so ​no ​lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding ​transition is ‌claimed. ​The editorial ‌work ​is to ​fix ​one ​reviewed reference ‌spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ​and ‌provenance, and ​keep ​the ‌original evidence ‌visible. ‌The displayed ‌form ​is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a ​description computed ​from ‌the displayed ​form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- **r** ​→ ​**R** — ‌Same
- ​**o** → ‌**o** ​— ‌Same
- **n** ​→ ‌**n** — ‌Same
- ​**g** → ​**g** ​— ​Same
- **o** ‌→ ‌**o** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/rongo/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**rongo** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Rongo.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Rongo" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Rongo" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"rongo" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Rongo ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Rongo ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Rongo ‌place ​agriculture, peace, ​cultivated ​foods at ​the ​center of ‌a ​living ​mythological world.

### ‌Origins ​(Myth)

Rongo ‌appears ​in polynesian ‌tradition ​as ​agriculture, peace, ​cultivated ​foods. The ​name's ‌meaning, ​"Peace, news ‌(from ​Proto-Polynesian *longo)", ‌shapes ​the narratives ‌told ​about ‌this figure.

### ​Worship ​and Memory ‌(Cult)

‌Devotees and ‌later ​tradition-keepers ​preserved Rongo ‌in ​ritual, text, ​and ‌iconography, ​ensuring the ​name ‌survived into ​the ‌modern scholarly ​record.

​The ​myths of ​Rongo ‌survive in ‌fragments, ​summaries, ‌and later ​retellings. ​Each version ‌reflects ‌the interests ‌of ‌its ​tellers — ‌poets, ​priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ‌PuniCodex ​entry ​does not ​privilege ‌a single ​version; ​it ​gathers the ‌attestations ​so that ‌readers ​can compare ‌them. ​The ‌restoration Rongo ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Rongo ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Polynesian ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Rongo, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​agriculture ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Rongo ​is the ‌god ‌of the ​planted ​world, and ​his ​theology is ​a parable ‌of ​gentle extraction. ​He ‌does not ​demand ‌conquest or ​ecstasy; ‌he asks ​that ​the earth ​be ​opened carefully, ​that ‌the first ​fruits be ‌returned, ​that peace ‌hold ​while the ‌crop ​ripens. In ‌an ​age that ​treats ‌food as ‌logistics, ‌Rongo remembers ​that ​eating is ‌a relationship ​— ​between the ‌digger ​and the ​hidden ‌god, between ​the ‌season of ​war ​and the ​season ​of the ‌storehouse.

His ‌pan-Polynesian ​name is ‌itself ​a map ​of ‌voyaging: wherever ‌the ‌canoes landed, ‌Rongo ​landed with ‌them, ​taking local ​form ​but keeping ‌his office. ​That ​a whole ​ocean ‌could agree ​on ​one quiet ​god ‌of the ​garden ‌says something ​the ‌loud gods ​never ‌manage: the ‌things that ​feed ​us are ​the ​things we ‌hold ‌most in ​common.[^1]
